To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) gender typicality and contentedness are positively associated with adjustment, whereas pressure and intergroup prejudice are negatively associated with adjustment, (b) the associations between the gender identity components and adjustment are independent of self-efficacies for gender-typed activities, (c) the gender identity components show some degree of stability across the school year, and (d) the gender identity constructs show different patterns of relations with adjustment in boys and girls.

the five components of gender identity are distinct and relatively stable, that gender identity components relate to adjustment in different ways, that these links remain significant when self-efficacy perceptions are controlled, and that the gender identity components are related to self-efficacy beliefs in different ways.

gender typicality and gender self-esteem are favorably related to self-esteem and peer status, whereas perceived pressure for conformity and intergroup bias are negatively associated with these adjustment variables.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and consequences of children's beliefs about gender, their gender identity, and their adjustment.
the nature and development of gender identity in middle childhood and its relation to adjustment.
the development of gender identity and gender role behavior.

gender identity is an important aspect of the development of the child and that gender identity is formed by a combination of biological factors (genetic and hormonal) and social factors.
the research conducted on gender identity and adjustment in childhood is not conclusive and is still inconclusive.
gender identity is a complex construct, and that the relationship between gender identity and adjustment is a complicated one.

the majority of children with a gender identity disorder are able to live in the gender role that is consistent with their biological sex and that they do not develop a transsexual identity in adulthood.

gender identity is a complex, multidimensional, and dynamic construct that is influenced by biological and environmental factors, as well as the individual’s own cognitive and social processing abilities.
